messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Conflict: Confrontations
  Maladaptive Strategies: Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tariq is a 41-year-old single man of Lebanese descent who works as a construction worker in a mid-sized city in the American Southwest. He came to the clinic with a PCL-5 score of 63, describing a life that had quietly contracted around him over the years until, as he put it, he could barely recognize the person he had become.

The trauma Tariq carries originates in his childhood home, where he spent years watching his father assault his mother — not occasionally, but with a regularity that gave the household a particular texture of dread. What he remembers is uneven and strange. Certain moments are photographically precise: the particular angle of his father's arm raised in the kitchen doorway, the pattern of the linoleum floor, the sound of something ceramic breaking. Other stretches are simply gone — whole evenings swallowed by blankness that he cannot voluntarily recover. When he tries to sit down and deliberately reconstruct what happened, the memory resists him, retreating behind a wall he cannot scale. Yet without warning, an image will surface with the clarity of a photograph — unbidden, complete, and devastating.

Those involuntary images are themselves triggers. A fragment of memory will arrive and, before Tariq can orient himself, his body is already responding: heart hammering, hands sweating, chest tightening as though the danger were present and immediate. These physical reactions are not metaphorical for him — they feel like genuine alarm. And the fragments, once activated, pull forward the full sensory weight of the original scenes, making the past feel porous and close. This mutual escalation between memory and physical reactivity has made Tariq deeply wary of anything that might disturb the fragile equilibrium he maintains day to day.

On the construction site, that vigilance is constant. Tariq works alongside foremen and site supervisors whose authority he consciously respects but whose presence — a raised voice, a pointed finger, a clipboard held with impatience — puts him immediately on edge. He finds himself scanning their faces and body language before they have said a word, reading for signs of anger or threat the way he once read his father's posture from across a room. When a delivery is late or a colleague takes too long returning from a break, Tariq's mind moves quickly toward catastrophe — something bad is unfolding, something is about to go wrong. This hypervigilance, while exhausting, feels to him entirely rational: he learned early that the gap between calm and violence could be very short.

When confrontations arise on the job — a disagreement about a measurement, a dispute over scheduling — Tariq withdraws. He has become known among his crew as someone who goes quiet, who defers, who will absorb an unfair criticism rather than push back. This avoidance of conflict has cost him professionally; a foreman's position he was offered two years ago he turned down, believing he could not manage the interpersonal friction the role would require. Away from work, he drifts. He describes a habit of retreating into an internal world of his own — daydreams, fantasies, extended reveries that can absorb hours — which began as a coping strategy in childhood and has never fully left him. He also finds himself dwelling on who he was before the weight of all this settled on him, an earlier version of himself that feels irretrievably distant. These strategies bring temporary relief, but they also keep him close to the emotional register of the trauma: the drifting and the dwelling stir up the very memories he is trying to escape, and those memories in turn reload his threat sensitivity and prime him to flinch at the next confrontation or unexpected delay. The loop is self-completing and has been for decades.

Talking about the future is its own particular difficulty. Any conversation that requires him to project forward — plans, hopes, commitments — produces a specific kind of dread he struggles to articulate. He has come to believe, without quite examining the belief, that the future is not a safe place to inhabit imaginatively.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a moment at a family gathering when a relative asked him a simple question about where he saw himself in five years, and he found he had no answer — not because he lacked ambition, but because the question produced such acute distress that he had to leave the room. He is most afraid that nothing will change. What he hopes, tentatively, is that someone can help him understand why he is still, at 41, standing in that kitchen doorway.
